The residents of Vegopia spend all their income on three vegetables: cauliflower, 
broccoli, and carrots. In 2010, they purchased 100 heads of cauliflower for $200, 50 
bunches of broccoli for $75, and 500 carrots for $50. In 2011, they purchased 75 
heads of cauliflower for $225, 80 bunches of broccoli for $120, and 500 carrots for 
$100.
a. Calculate the price of each vegetable in 2010 and 2011.
b. Using 2010 as the base year, calculate the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for each 
year.
c. Calculate the inflation rate in 2011.

a. Calculate the price per unit of electricity, per LPG cylinder, and per litre of petrol in 2024 
and 2025.

WHAT IS
PRODUCTIVITY? 
Productivity is the quantity of goods and services produced 
per unit of labour input.

WHY IS PRODUCTIVITY
IMPORTANT? 
• Higher productivity can increase output per worker.
• Higher output can support higher real incomes.
• Businesses may expand and create employment opportunities.
• Society can consume more goods and services with available 
resources.
• Sustained productivity growth can improve living standards over time.

FOUR DETERMINANTS
OF PRODUCTIVITY

CAN NATURAL RESOURCES ALONE
MAKE A COUNTRY RICH?
Natural resources can create wealth, but a country's long-term prosperity 
also depends on how productively it uses its workers, technology, capital 
and resources.

What can government policy do to raise productivity and living standards?
1. Saving and 
investment
Government investment in highways, railways, and 
industrial facilities.
Investment creates productive assets. Better transport allows 
businesses to move goods faster and reduce costs.
2. Physical 
capital PM GatiShakti infrastructure planning in India. Coordinating road, rail, port, and logistics projects can reduce 
delays and improve the movement of goods. 
3. Human 
capital 
(education)

training.
Students acquire skills that help them operate machinery, write 
software, solve engineering problems, and become more

4. Health and 
nutrition
Public healthcare, vaccination, nutrition 
programmes, and sanitation.
Healthier workers can attend work more regularly and perform 
tasks more effectively.
5. Foreign 
direct 
investment 
(FDI)
Hyundai Motor Group's announced $15.5 billion 
investment plan in India through 2032, reported in 
October 2026.
Foreign investment can expand manufacturing capacity, support

planned investments, not all completed expenditure.

Indian businesses exporting medicines,

university-industry collaboration.

10. Manufacturing

India's Production Linked Incentive 
(PLI) schemes.

Better resource management can improve

12. Population and

Skill-development programmes and

Workers gain skills and access to jobs, allowing the

Startup support, business registration

Bonds and stocks: debt versus ownership
BOND = DEBT FINANCE STOCK = EQUITY FINANCE
Bondholders lend, and shareholders own.
1. Meaning: You lend money to a company.

4. Risk: Generally less risky than shares, but you may lose

5. Your role: You are a lender (creditor), not an owner.

What makes bonds different?
SAVING, INVESTMENT & THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM 7
TERM / MATURITY
How long until the principal is repaid? Longer-term bonds often pay more to 
compensate for added risk. (Longer time = higher interest.)
CREDIT RISK
How likely is the borrower to miss interest or principal payments? 
Higher perceived default risk generally requires a higher rate. (HIGH 
RISK= higher interest.)
TAX TREATMENT
How is interest taxed? Tax advantages can allow some bonds to offer 
lower interest rates. (HIGH TAX= higher interest.)

How the interest rate restores equilibrium
14
Interest rate below equilibrium
• Quantity supplied is less than

• A shortage of loanable funds

• Quantity supplied exceeds

• Interest rates are pushed

Policy 1 • Incentives to Save
18
The government provides tax benefits on eligible savings or
retirement investments.
1. People find saving more attractive.
2. Supply of loanable funds increases (shifts right).
3. The equilibrium real interest rate falls.
4. Businesses can borrow more cheaply and investment 
increases.
Saving incentives → lower interest rate → higher investment.

Policy 3 • Budget Deficits And Crowding Out
18
The government collects ₹100 crore in taxes but spends ₹130
crore. It has a deficit of ₹30 crore and borrows to finance it.
1. The government spends more money than it collects in taxes, so it 
borrows money.
2. This reduces the money available for lending in the economy.
3. Interest rates go up because money becomes harder to get.
4. Businesses may avoid taking loans because borrowing becomes 
expensive. As a result, they may invest less in new factories and 
machines.
Budget deficit → lower national saving → higher interest rate →
lower private investment.

Economic Principles
CONCLUSION
• Economic principles explain how limited resources are allocated efficiently.
• Scarcity forces individuals and organizations to make choices.
• Opportunity cost highlights the value of alternatives that are given up.
• Supply and demand determine market prices and production levels.
• Marginal thinking and incentives improve decision-making.
• Productivity and market efficiency support long-term economic growth.
